I found this recipe on the side of a bag of sugar. It's nothing too special and it's the only sugar cookie recipe I've been using for years now, but if anyone has any suggestions on how to improve the recipe please share.

  • 1 cup butter (room temp)

  • 2 1/4 cups all purpose flour

  • 1 cup granulated white sugar

  • 1 egg

  • 1/2 teaspoon baking soda

  • 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract

In a bowl mix together butter and sugar and beat until fluffy.

Beat in the egg and vanilla extract.

Once everything is well mixed begin adding in the dry ingredients. (the flour and baking soda should be added simultaneously so simply mixing the 1/2 teaspoon with the 2 1/4 cups is recommended)

If you mix the dough by hand like me you're going to have a bad time. The process can take anywhere from 10-20 minutes by hand simply due to taking small breaks.

Seriously, hand cramps will happen. If you have one of those $200 Kitchen-Aid mixers do yourself a favor...

Once the dough is evenly mixed, separate it into two even halves and drop them onto some wax paper and roll each dough half up until they have about a 2.5 inch diameter. (the official recipe says wax paper but in my experience the dough comes out just slightly too goopy to effectively roll up so I just use 2 large zip-loc freezer bags for both halves, however if your dough is manageable by all means use the paper)

Place the rolls in the refrigerator for a little over an hour to harden. Or stick them in the freezer for just under an hour if you have no time to lose.

Preheat your oven to 375 degrees.

Remove dough from the fridge, unwrap and slice your cookies to 1/4 inch thickness.

Bake on an ungreased cookie sheet for 8 to 12 minutes. Let them cool as you please.

There you have it. Bear in mind I got this recipe off the side of a store brand bag of sugar so it certainly isn't the best but definitely not the worst. What do you think of this recipe?

I would be interested in hearing what stance atheists (or theists, deists, etc.) take on "right to death".

"Right to death" refers to an individuals choice to take their life if they are terminally ill or if their elder spouse will pass away (I can't think of other scenarios but there probably are).

I am one hundred percent in favor of it. I think it's inhumane to force someone to suffer through a long, drawn out, undignified dying process when assisted suicide is readily available. As it stands, people who will die soon often sign DNR's, which basically means that when their heart or lungs start to give they won't receive any assistance. This leads to very painful, terrible deaths which could be avoided if we as a society could collectively get over this idea that ending your life is inherently bad. Sometimes a syringe full of morphine is the best of a bunch of terrible options.

I also agree with preventing a possible horrible life through abortion. We abort down syndrome fetuses, and women/families often make the choice to have an abortion when the life outcomes for that child would be detrimental in the long run.

In a time where problems are often caused by excess, we can prevent ills by making informed choices about life and death (in a non eugenics manner), with family planning and humane euthanasia.

I'm an Athiest, and I'm pro choice. I wouldn't encourage anyone to kill themselves but I'm not for it being completely against the law. On a larger scale, I'm not for much of anything to be completely against the law. I feel when you ban something you give up all control over it. If someone wants to kill themselves, they can, in extremely violent and messy ways. Maybe if it was legal, and there was a waiting period and you could just take a pill, get a shot, go to sleep and never wake up it. That's better than someone coming home and finding a body, right? Maybe that waiting period has some therapy involved, or possibly a doctor. Maybe it's long enough from them to have a change of heart, and just the fact that there was a legal avenue that they would go down, could identify the leading cause. And if they go through all of that, then they are obviously secure in their decision.

I don't believe in an afterlife, so this is our one chance, I think we make the most of it and not end it prematurely, but I'm for people making their own choices whether they align with mine or not.

but I'm for people making their own choices whether they align with mine or not.

May add that I don;t care if your Choices align with mine or not, as long as they do not impede my choice, and Vice Versa.

Euthanasia of a reasonable adult should not be illegal. I do agree however, that some process needs to be in place to make sure that your decision is indeed reasonable, otherwise a lot of people with otherwise treatable problems will end their lives unnecessarily
But if a person and their family and their doctor decide it's time for them to go, what can the government add to that equation? Over regulation can have the same effect as an outright ban.
If a person, their family and their doctor decide, then that is the exact kind of oversight I am talking about.

I know those were the terms I just listed, but even now I am rethinking the idea of family involvement. What if the doctor and patient both agree that euthanasia is the right course, but the family disagrees. Do their rights supersede the patient's? What if the patient, doctor, father, sister, and wife all agree but the mother doesn't?

Perhaps a Doctor assessing if a patient is 'of Sound Mind' is all that is required.

If you have made your wishes, your family might just have to live with it. If you are unable to make that decision, due to coma or similar, then you should have the right to lay out those wishes in a will. If you are in testate, then I suppose the decision lies with the next of kin, unless you have prepared a pwer of attorney. Laws need to be made to say that the documents are final and cannot be contested.

I'm not sure I am necessarily an Atheist, but I don't believe in punishment or anything after death (nor the deity that requires it). I've spoken about this book in my past comments and I'll refer to it again, here. This quote is from "God" in Conversations With God, Book 3:

With you, it seems to be merely a question of time. The legality of self-destruction—the "rightness" or "wrongness" of it—seems to have much to do with how quickly the deed is done, as well as who is doing it. The faster the death, the more "wrong" it seems to be. The slower the death, the more it slips into "okayness."

Interestingly, this is the exact opposite of what a truly humane society would conclude. By any reasonable definition of what you would call "humane," the shorter the death, the better. Yet your society punishes those who would seek to do the humane thing, and rewards those who would do the insane.

It's my go to "bible" and it directly reflects how I felt about most things before I ever read it. So I guess my opinion would be that ultimate freedom is truly being able to make every choice, about yourself, for yourself, without prejudice.

As it stands, many people do exercise their right to take their own lives at present. We are our own beings, and ours is our own destiny to fufill. The problem as it stands is many who wish to exercise this right are no longer in a physical state to be able to, and many in the physical state to achieve the desired outcome are not in the mental state to be making such a terminal decision.

As long as some kind of checks and balances are in place in order to make sure that the person choosing to exercise their "Right to Death" is of sound and reasonable mind to make it, I have no problem. We ensure the same soundness of mind for many other "Rights" (driving and gun ownership are two that I can think of. We even ensure that people are of sound mind before they can sign a loan contract) so I see no problem with some kind of medical assesment and evaluation before a reasonable person can exercise this right.

Death with dignity is a concept that I'm struggling with right this very moment. I work in mental health and that makes it even more complicated since it is difficult to categorize any mental illness as "terminal" even when accounting for suicide. Even if a person is in severe psychological distress, I will always believe that that person's mental state can be improved through excellent and consistent mental health treatment. There is always, always, always hope.

But who is to say that a person should strive for happiness or at least a lessening of their pain for the rest of their life? If a person is mentally tortured practically every single day, who is to say that that person should not be able to determine his or her own fate? I know that we're talking about mental illness here but I think it is important to note that just because a person is struggling with mental illness does not necessarily make them incompetent or incapable of logical thought or insight. A lot of times they are, but that is a matter for the individual and their treatment team to decide.

I suppose one could argue that if a person really wanted to die, that no one could stop them. But why does it have to be so painful? If that person does not want to try to get better anymore (especially if they've genuinely tried their best to get better over a long period of time), why should society stop them? Indeed, why not help to ease that person's suffering?

I'm an atheist but I'm not sure how much that has to do with my feelings about this topic.

Atheist here. I may be outside of the regular thought process but I think not only should the sick and elderly have the right to death with dignity, but everyone should. You get one life and you choose how you want to live it. If you are perfectly healthy and decide you don't like what life offers you, you should be free to end it. Sadly, many people are forced to do this alone and in terrible ways. It would be nice for them to have an option more comfortable, humane and controlled so we can reuse their parts they don't want.

That said, I fell like there should be sufficient screening processes to avoid people just in a funk choosing death. I don't know what those screening processes should be, but I guess I don't have to think about it very hard. No law or service like this will ever pass.

Personally, as an atheist, my one life is the single most valuable thing I own. I only get one and it might end any moment without warning. When it ends, you get nothing. So it is best to use this time wisely. But if someone decides to throw a perfectly good life away, that is their choice. We can use their parts to save others who want to live.
